newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin raps "terrorism" in graveside bomb killing.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin raps "terrorism" in graveside bomb killing.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin condemned a bloody attack by gangland bombers as "terrorism" on Monday as Russia ordered special teams to find the killers of 13 mourners at a Moscow cemetery.
The explosion, at noon on Sunday, was the bloodiest manifestation so far in a battle for control between rival criminal gangs in the new post-Soviet Russia.

Investigators said the killing was linked to a longstanding feud between two rival branches of the five-year-old Afghan War Invalids' Foundation, a charity set up to help disabled victims of the Afghan war.
Yeltsin, recovering from a quintuple heart bypass operation, said in a statement released by his press office he had ordered authorities to investigate the blast.

"I learned with grief about the terrorist act at the Kotlyakovskoye cemetery in Moscow," said Yeltsin. "I express my condolences to the relatives and close friends of those who were killed. I have ordered the legal authorities to carry out a thorough investigation of all the details of this bloody crime."
The Moscow prosecutor's office said the attack was being probed as terrorism and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov said he was taking special charge of the hunt.

Members of the State Duma lower house of parliament held a minute's silence in respect for the dead. "Even in the current conditions of arbitrary crime, this crime goes beyond all limits," Interfax quoted one Duma deputy as saying.
The blast hurled one body some 30 metres (yards) into the air. The victims included the mother and the widow of the man being commemorated, himself killed by a bomb two years ago.
The deputies asked prosecutors to open a full investigation into the charity and some politicians said it was time for a crackdown on tax breaks enjoyed by non-profit organisations.

Some analysts say the breaks have deprived the authorities of billions of dollars in tax revenue. Many perks have been scrapped, but low tax revenues remain one of Russia's biggest economic headaches.
Rising crime worries many in the new capitalist Russia and solving the lawlessness will be crucial for Yeltsin when he recovers fully from his operation and returns to work.

Yeltsin, 65, has spent only a handful of days in the Kremlin since he was re-elected for a second term in office on July 3. But doctors say he is recovering well from the bypass operation and they expect him back at work soon.
The Kremlin said Yeltsin would speak to the nation this week, but a spokesman did not make clear what the address would be about or if it would be on radio or television.

Yeltsin, who made several radio addresses to the nation before his operation, last spoke on television on October 17, signing a decree sacking maverick security chief Alexander Lebed in front of the cameras.

The bomb blast was the latest in a series of explosions and gangland murders to rock Moscow, where the transition to a market economy has generated a spate of unsolved contract killings of prominent businessmen, bankers and officials.

U.S. businessman Paul Tatum, locked in a dispute with Russian partners over ownership of a Moscow hotel where U.S. President Bill Clinton has stayed, died in a hail of bullets at the entrance to a nearby underground station on November 3.

U.S. business leaders in Moscow said at the time that the murder, which bore the hallmark of a contract killing, could hurt Russia's chances of attracting foreign capital as it tries to revive ailing companies and reverse a long and painful decline in industrial output.
